message.reasoning: This is a tricky task since TokeniserState is package-private, so my tests need to live in org.jsoup.parser and rely on real Tokeniser/CharacterReader instances rather than mocks, since no mockito is available. I recall that in jsoup, Tokeniser and CharacterReader are both package-private classes with package-private constructors, so testing likely needs to go through the public Jsoup.parse() API to indirectly exercise TokeniserState transitions, or construct these objects directly since the test class resides in the same package and has access. This could also be black-box testing through the public Jsoup.parse API, which indirectly exercises many tokeniser states and branches. I'm planning to write test methods covering various HTML constructs - comments, doctype, CDATA, script/rawtext/rcdata sections, attribute parsing, character references, null chars and EOF edge cases - while checking what constructors and access levels are actually available for CharacterReader and Tokeniser within the same package. Since the read method is package-private, I can call TokeniserState.Data.read(tokeniser, reader) directly from a test in the same package for precise branch coverage. I need to recall Tokeniser's internal fields and helper methods like createTagPending, createCommentPending, transition, and emit to properly construct test scenarios. But manually driving each state through direct read() calls would require deep access to internal fields like tagPending and dataBuffer, which gets complex fast. Given the realistic scope of this task, I suspect the better approach is to test through the public API instead -- parsing HTML with Jsoup.parse() and verifying the resulting Document structure, which indirectly exercises these tokenizer states. I'll write tests using Jsoup.parse() calls that check tag names, attributes, text, comments, and doctype output across varied HTML snippets to cover the relevant branches. I also recall real jsoup test cases like testUnconsumeAfterBufferUp, testOpeningAngleBracketInsteadOfTag, and testUnconsumeIgnoresNulls that might be relevant here. Since I don't know the exact diff for this specific bug ID, I'll avoid guessing specifics and instead write a broad, comprehensive suite using both the public Jsoup.parse API and direct package-private access to CharacterReader and Tokeniser for simpler states like Data, PLAINTEXT, CdataSection, and Bogus Comment. I'm planning around 25-35 test methods aiming for solid branch coverage, mapping tokenizer states to crafted HTML inputs -- like testing ampersand handling for character references, tag-open transitions, and null character emission in the Data state. For TagOpen I'm covering markup declaration ("and EOF-in-comment scenarios, then the various CommentEnd branches (extra dash, bang, null char, default), followed by Doctype parsing -- handling whitespace before the name, empty "" cases, and what happens when a character immediately follows "DOCTYPE" without a space. I realize the 'h' character gets consumed as the trigger in Doctype.read's default branch but never stored since createDoctypePending isn't called there - meaning it's lost, which could be a quirk worth testing explicitly. Now moving to examine BeforeDoctypeName's behavior with matchesLetter. For BeforeDoctypeName I also need to test the null char case, eof handling, and the default case for a non-letter non-null character. Then DoctypeName needs coverage for matchesLetter consuming sequences, the '>' emit case, whitespace transitioning to AfterDoctypeName, null char, and eof. AfterDoctypeName needs tests for isEmpty/eof, whitespace advancing, the '>' case, detecting the PUBLIC keyword with quoted identifiers, detecting SYSTEM keyword, and falling through to bogus doctype for anything else. Next I'm planning CDATA section tests, verifying no exception is thrown and that "Hello" content shows up somewhere in the output. Then I'm covering script data escape states -- normal scripts, comment-escape, double-escape matching against the "script" keyword, and the fallback branch when the buffer doesn't match "script". Finally I'm mapping out which tags to use for testing Rawtext, Rcdata, ScriptData, and Plaintext states. For PLAINTEXT specifically, I'm checking that everything after the opening tag is treated as literal text with no further tag parsing, so tags like "world" should appear unparsed in the body. Given the scope, I'm aiming for roughly 35-40 focused test methods, mixing Jsoup.parse with error tracking where relevant and plain parsing otherwise, while flagging uncertain assumptions like the RcdataLessthanSign divergence branch and exact BogusComment output format. I still need to confirm the exact jsoup public API names I'll be using. Since the test class sits in the same package as the parser internals, I could directly reference Tokeniser and CharacterReader without imports to test lower-level edge cases like empty string handling precisely, but given time constraints I'll keep things simpler. I'd rather avoid guessing at exact constructor signatures for internal classes like ParseErrorList, since getting those wrong risks compile failures. It's safer to stick entirely to the stable, documented public API—Jsoup, Parser, and the nodes package—to minimize the chance of errors from assuming internal behavior that isn't actually in the source. Setting up the test class imports... For error tracking tests, I'll use Parser.htmlParser() with setTrackErrors enabled, parse the input, then check the returned error list is populated - both Parser and ParseError live in the same package so no extra imports are needed. Now I'm planning out the full set of roughly 32 test methods to cover, starting with testData. Now I'm drafting the complete list of test method names covering the data state, tag open state, and end tag open state transitions - things like handling plain text, ampersand entities, null chars, EOF cases, comment/bogus-comment starts, tag name starts, and various error conditions for malformed markup. Continuing into tag name and attribute state tests: self-closing tags, null char replacement, EOF before closing, whitespace transitioning to attribute parsing, and then a full set covering attribute value quoting styles (double, single, unquoted), boolean attributes, entities in values, null chars, empty values, and backtick errors in unquoted attributes. I'm also listing missing whitespace errors, invalid characters after self-closing slashes, markup declaration handling for doctype and CDATA sections, bogus comments, and a thorough set of comment state tests covering basic comments, empty dash-dash sequences, premature closes, null chars, unterminated EOF, and the bang transition in comment-end state. This rolls into doctype tests starting with basic HTML5 doctypes, empty doctype quirks mode, and public identifier handling. I'm deciding to trim the full list of ~49 tests down to a more manageable ~35-40, keeping each one simple with lenient assertions since I'm not fully certain of the tokenizer's exact output nuances—better to check key substrings than enforce overly strict comparisons. I need to be careful with escaping quotes and backslashes in the Java string literals used for the HTML attribute test fixtures, and I'll add comments flagging assumptions where exact output format (like bogus comment content or CDATA rendering) is uncertain, sometimes falling back to just verifying parsing doesn't throw. For the test with input "< foo bar", tracing through TagOpen.read: the character after '<' isn't '!', '/', or '?', and since it's not a letter either, this triggers an error and emits a literal '<' before transitioning back to Data state, which then reads " foo bar" as text. Since jsoup merges adjacent text nodes in the tree builder, the resulting body text should end up combined as "< foo bar". Since text() trims leading/trailing but not internal whitespace, this should produce "< foo bar" fine, and the full document wrapping with html/body won't affect the body text content. Now I'm moving to the nullChar test for Data reading, where a string contains a literal null character and the expected behavior is that the tokenizer errors but still emits the null character itself. This exact text equality check is too risky, so I'll just verify that parsing doesn't throw and that the errors list has at least one entry, using `doc.body().html()` loosely rather than strict string matching. I'll apply this same lighter assertion style to other tricky edge cases too. Now I'm sketching helper methods: one to run the parser with error tracking enabled and return the collected errors, and another to just parse and return the Document separately for structural checks. Then I'm writing individual test cases, starting with plain text consumption and ampersand entity handling, checking that the parsed document text matches expectations. Adding more test cases... Adding more test cases... I'm checking what happens at EOF when the input is just "", building up the final tag name as "di" plus the replacement character plus "v". I'm writing a test that parses an HTML string with a null byte embedded in the tag name and checks that the resulting element's tagName equals "di" followed by the Unicode replacement character and "v", confirming the lowercase letters stay intact and the null gets swapped for U+FFFD. Then I draft a test for an unclosed tag like "" triggers an error and forces quirks mode. Adding more doctype tests... Adding a test for bogus tokens after the doctype name, checking that an error is raised and forceQuirks mode kicks in while parsing still succeeds. Now I'm moving to RCDATA/Rawtext/ScriptData/Plaintext tests, covering `` parsing with entity decoding, literal `<` characters that don't match an end tag, and null character handling that should trigger a parse error. I'm then writing tests for `<style>` rawtext content, basic `<script>` parsing with embedded `<`, script comment-escape sequences, and starting a test for double-escape handling with the "script" keyword inside script data. Adding more test cases... Writing more RCDATA tests... Tracing through the state machine step by step: the '/' advances into RCDATAEndTagOpen, which checks without consuming whether '1' is a letter -- it isn't, so it emits "</" and drops back to Rcdata without consuming that '1'. The next read then grabs "1>b" as plain data since '>' doesn't stop consumption in Rcdata, giving the accumulated text "a</1>b" before the real closing "" tag is finally encountered. The second time through, the character after '/' is 't', which does match a letter, so RCDATAEndTagOpen now behaves differently -- it creates a pending tag, appends 't' to both the tag name and data buffer, and transitions into RCDATAEndTagName to collect the rest of "title" as a genuine end tag. Since the tag pending name "title" matches the last start tag emitted, isAppropriateEndTagToken() returns true, so the tag is emitted and we transition back to Data state, properly closing the title element. This gives a final title text of "ab", which still contains "" and satisfies my assertion -- I'll keep this test with a comment explaining the appropriateEndTagName reasoning, then move on to testing the other RcdataLessthanSign diverge branch where the letter doesn't match an appropriate closing tag. Since I can't be fully certain of appropriateEndTagName's exact internal logic from the given source, I'll mark this test as uncertain and focus on verifying no crash occurs for an input like "before<b>middle", reasoning through how the tokenizer would traverse the RcdataLessthanSign state for the embedded "" tag. Since it actually finds "beforenever closes" with no closing tag anywhere — then containsIgnoreCase returns false, the condition flips true, and it auto-emits an end tag for "title", unconsumes, and transitions to Data. I'm now writing a test case for this scenario. Adding another test case for when the closing tag name doesn't match the original RCDATA start tag—since "span" isn't the appropriate end tag for "title", the parser treats it as literal text and stays in Rcdata state, so the title content ends up containing "" rather than closing early. Then the real closing "" matches appropriately, giving a final title text of "xy" — confirming my assertion. I've verified this reasoning holds for the earlier RCDATAEndTagOpen non-letter case too, and I think I have enough coverage now; I'll settle on roughly 45 well-organized test methods covering the remaining branches like AttributeName null chars and BeforeAttributeName quote cases, which feels appropriately thorough without being excessive. Adding more test cases... I also want a test confirming that a stray letter after an attribute name correctly starts a new attribute rather than merging into the previous one. That should round out the test list. Still writing test class...
